rows.text: Dmitri Meshin
Fractional Chief AI Officer
Platform engineer by trade. My work is getting an AI system past a corporate security review and into production, then handing it to the team that has to run it.
ISO/IEC 42001 Lead Implementer — PECB course in progress, exam not taken yet

I work with companies of thirty to three hundred people who have run a few AI pilots and cannot get one into production. The blocker is rarely the model. It is who owns the risk, which data may reach a vendor, and whether anyone would notice if a prompt change made the output worse.
only.help — agentic support triage, on my own product
An agentic support triage workflow that went from a demo notebook to a production path with evals in CI and a named owner.

My own product
A support inbox growing faster than the people reading it, and a prototype agent nobody would let near a real customer because there was no way to tell whether an answer was good.

Pick the one flow with volume and a measurable outcome, build an eval set from real tickets before touching the prompt, then put the eval run in CI so a regression blocks the merge rather than the customer.

## Why this one first The inbox was the only place where volume and a measurable outcome met. Every other candidate needed a survey to tell whether it had worked, and a metric you have to ask about is a metric you cannot gate a release on. ## What made it shippable Three things, in this order. An eval set built from tickets that had already been answered, so there was a known-good answer to compare against. Tracing on every call, so a bad answer could be traced to the retrieval step rather than argued about. A cost ceiling per ticket, checked in the same CI job as the evals. ## What I built, in order | Part | What it's for | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Eval set from real tickets | A known-good answer to check every change against, before it reaches a customer. | | [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) as the tool boundary | Keeps what the agent is allowed to call explicit and narrow, instead of improvised inside a prompt. | | [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) tracing | Every call recorded, so a wrong answer traces back to a retrieval step, not a guess. | | GitHub Actions eval gate | Runs the eval set on every change so a regression blocks the merge before it reaches a ticket. | ## What I would do differently I built the first eval set from tickets that had already been answered well. Seasonality made the first week of results look better than the system was. Sampling across a longer window would have caught that before anyone celebrated.
Are models trained on our customer data?

Not by default. I use vendor terms that exclude your data from model training, the same enterprise or business-tier terms a compliance team would ask about, and I check that clause before any tool touches your data. If a vendor will not commit to that in writing, that tool does not get used on your systems.
Can you get us certified to ISO/IEC 42001, or do you just build a working system?
Can you get us ISO/IEC 42001 certified?
Certification comes from an accredited body after an independent audit, not from me: my work gets your management system and evidence trail audit-ready.

An accredited certification body issues certification after an independent audit, and I am not the one who runs it. My work is built to get your management system, risk register, and evidence trail to the point an auditor would recognise as ready. Whether you then pursue ISO/IEC 42001 certification itself is a separate decision, best made once you can see the system actually running.
Can you work with our existing AI vendor or platform, or do you bring your own tools?
Can you work with our existing AI vendor?

I work with what you already run: OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, or whatever your team picked before I arrived. The Retainer does not require a vendor switch. What changes is the governance layer around the tools you keep. That means a data flow review, contract terms checked for training exclusions, and evals wrapped around workflows already running, not a rebuild from scratch.
How do you charge for the work?

Three fixed structures, no hourly billing. The Assessment is a fixed fee for the two weeks. The Sprint is quoted once, from the scope in the statement of work. The Retainer is a monthly fee for one or two days a week. You hear the number on the fit call, and it is written down before any work starts, so there is no surprise invoice partway through.
How does AI risk get recorded, and who signs it off?

In an AI register: one line per initiative, its data flows, its risk level, and its owner. Under the Retainer, I review every entry and sign it as the named officer; final accountability for anything that reaches customers or the board still sits with your organisation, the same as for any other risk register you keep.
How does the Retainer end?

With a named internal owner in place and the decisions that got made written down, not with a call that quietly stops getting returned. The handover plan exists from the first month, not the last. A retainer running past two years would mean the design was wrong; the plan is written to end well before that.
How is a prompt or model change stopped from shipping unnoticed?
How is a prompt or model change caught?

Evals in continuous integration: a test set that runs on every change and fails the build when quality drops, the same gate your engineers already trust for code. A prompt edit, a model swap, a vendor's silent update: all pass the same evals as the original release before reaching production. Tracing shows what changed.
How is cost per outcome measured?

On a dashboard built during the Sprint. Total spend on the workflow, model calls included, divided by how many times it produced the outcome. You define that outcome before the Sprint starts. The number sits next to tracing. So when it moves, you can see why: volume, a model change, or a real quality problem.
How quickly can you start, and how does availability work for a remote officer?
How quickly can you start as a remote officer?

One client gets one or two days a week at a time, which is what makes me actually reachable instead of spread across five accounts. I work remote worldwide, so time zones are just a scheduling detail. Book a fit call to check current availability; if the timing is wrong, I will tell you rather than stall.
Is my company too small, or too early, for a Fractional Chief AI Officer?
Is my company too small for a Fractional CAIO?

Size isn't the real test. If you're running pilots that never reach production, or a customer or investor has already asked who owns your AI risk, you're ready. If you have no engineers, no pilots, and nobody outside the company has asked that question yet, you're early: fix that first, then book a call.
What counts as 'in production' for the 90-day Sprint?

Real users or real transactions, monitored, with a rollback path and someone on call — that is the bar. A demo behind a feature flag does not clear it, and neither does a workflow only your team tried. The success measure gets written into the statement of work before the Sprint starts, so whether it actually shipped is settled before the work even begins.
What do NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act each require of a company our size?
What do NIST, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act require?

None of the three sets a headcount threshold. NIST's AI RMF is voluntary guidance built around four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable standard for running an AI management system. The EU AI Act is binding law: what you owe depends on being a provider (building AI into what you sell) or a deployer (only using it inside the business), plus the system's risk tier, not your size.
What do we do about tools staff are already using without approval?
What about tools staff use without approval?

Put them in the register rather than pretend they aren't there; banning them after the fact just pushes the same behaviour further underground. The Retainer's first step is exactly this. Inventory the AI tools and data flows already in the building, then a data classification and an acceptable-use policy your engineers can actually follow.
What does a Fractional Chief AI Officer actually do, and how is that different from an advisor?
What does a Fractional Chief AI Officer do?

I carry the AI risk register, review every initiative, sign the answers to security questionnaires, and sit in design reviews, all as a named officer on your side. An advisor gives an opinion and leaves; I own the outcome and answer for it. A week usually holds a security questionnaire, a design review, and a page for the board.
What does the two-week Assessment produce, and is the fee credited if we continue?
What does the two-week Assessment produce?

A memo your board can act on: a readiness score across strategy, data, delivery, people and governance, a gap list against NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act, and three processes ranked by what automating them is worth this quarter. Yes: if you move to the 90-Day Sprint within three months, the full Assessment fee is credited off the Sprint price.
What happens if the evals say a workflow isn't good enough?
What if the evals say a workflow is not enough?

Then it does not ship. The Sprint ends with a written account of why the workflow fell short and what would need to change, instead of a launch that quietly under-performs until a customer notices. That is a cheaper outcome than shipping it, and the eval numbers decide it, whatever the deadline is.
What happens on a fit call, and does it cost anything?

It costs nothing and runs thirty minutes, booked at cal.com/meshin. Tell me about the process you want in production, who owns it today and your timeline. By the end you will know whether an Assessment, a Sprint or neither is the right next step — no slide deck required.
What if the AI we're building goes into a product we sell, not just an internal workflow?
What if our AI goes into a product we sell?

Both are covered, and the obligations differ. Building AI into a product you sell can make your company a provider rather than a deployer under the EU AI Act. That carries a higher compliance bar than using AI only inside the business. I record that distinction in the risk register from the first review, so it gets decided early, not discovered after the feature has shipped.
What if we already have a data science team or an internal AI lead?
What if we already have a data science team?

Your data science team stays exactly where it is: I do not write models, tune pipelines, or manage engineers. What I bring is different. I own the AI risk register as the named officer, I sign the procurement answers, and I report to the board on AI decisions. A company of your size usually has the technical people already; what it lacks is someone accountable for AI outside the team itself.
What size of company do you actually work with?

Companies of thirty to three hundred people, usually with at least one engineer. Most have run AI pilots that stalled before production. Below that size, the process volume and engineering capacity are rarely there yet. Above it, you usually have an internal AI leader already and need something else.
What's the difference between the Assessment, the Sprint and the Retainer?
Assessment, Sprint or Retainer: what differs?

The Assessment is two weeks at a fixed fee, and ends in a memo on where you stand and what to fix first. The Sprint is 90 days at a fee quoted from the agreed scope, and puts one agentic workflow live in production with evals and a rollback path. The Retainer is a monthly fee, one or two days a week, as your named AI officer. If unsure, start with the Assessment.
Who answers customer security questionnaires?

I do, as the named officer on record. That is a core part of the Retainer: procurement answers and questionnaire responses as they arrive, backed by the AI register and the acceptable-use policy, so the answers match what is actually running.
Who owns the code and the data?

You do, both. The code lives in your repositories from the first commit, under your licence and your review rules, and the same principle applies to your data: nothing about the engagement moves ownership of either to me or to a vendor. What can change hands is access, temporarily and by agreement, for the work that needs it.
Who owns the frameworks, templates and playbooks built during the engagement?
Who owns the frameworks and playbooks I build?

Everything written for your business — the register, the policies, the runbooks — belongs to you, the same as your code and data do. What stays mine is the method: how I structure an assessment, build eval templates and run a risk review. I reuse that method with other clients, never your specific content, your data or your configuration.
Why hire a fractional officer instead of a full-time head of AI?
Why hire a fractional officer over a full-time head?

A named officer on your customers' security reviews and your board's roadmap — that is the accountability you get, without a full-time salary, a hiring process, or a seat that sits empty between AI decisions. If you need someone hands-on across five systems at once, that is a full-time hire, not a Retainer.
What is an agentic workflow?
Agentic workflow
An agentic workflow is a task run by one or more LLM agents that plan steps, call tools and decide what happens next.

An agentic workflow is a task one or more AI agents complete on their own once started. The system plans steps, calls tools or APIs, checks the result, and decides what happens next without a person approving each move.

The distinction that matters is between a single prompt and response and a task an agent sees through to the end. A chatbot that answers one question is not agentic. A system that reads a support ticket, looks up the order, drafts a refund and issues it, is agentic: nobody scripted that exact sequence in advance. Engineering teams build this pattern because it automates the cross-system judgement calls that used to need a person. Security reviewers and boards ask about it separately from the model itself, because the risk changes once a system can act, not only speak. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing. A wrong action against a live order or a payment has already happened by the time anyone notices, because nothing stood between the decision and the outcome.

## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a pitch or a product description says "agent" instead of "assistant". A security reviewer's next question is almost always what the agent can do without asking first, since that is where the real exposure sits, not the model choice. A board hears "agentic" and correctly hears "this thing takes actions on its own." That is a different risk conversation than a chatbot that only produces text. ## What to do about it List every action an agent can take, not just what it can say, and sign off on each as a separate risk. Set a real limit on what it can do without a person confirming first, especially anything that spends money, touches a customer record, or sends something external. Log every tool call, so a bad outcome traces to a specific decision. Evals belong here: test the whole action chain, not just the model's replies.
What is AI governance?
AI governance
AI governance is the decisions, roles and controls a company uses to manage the risk of the AI systems it builds or buys.

AI governance is the accountability layer above an AI system - who is allowed to build or buy it, and who answers, by name, when it fails. It runs through the policies, roles and controls that decide what data a system may touch and who signs off before it reaches customers.

AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. That shows up as a register of the systems in use, a policy engineers actually follow, and a review step before anything new goes live. A customer's procurement team asks for it during a security review. A board asks after a pilot nears production, once someone raises who is liable for a bad call. Regulators ask for pieces of it too, through frameworks like the NIST AI RMF and standards like ISO/IEC 42001. In practice, it changes three things. Someone specific owns each AI system, instead of it belonging to whichever team built it. A new system needs sign-off before it touches customer data. A written answer exists the day a customer or auditor asks for one.

## Why it comes up An insurer asks who owns AI risk before writing a policy. A board member reads about an AI failure elsewhere and asks what would happen here. An investor's due-diligence checklist now has a line for it too. Write down who is responsible for each system, and who would notice if it started producing worse answers. ## What to do about it Start with a one-page register: every AI system in use, who owns it, what data it touches, and whether customer data leaves the building. Assign one named owner per system, not a team. Add a single sign-off step before a new system reaches production. Map what you already do against the NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001, not to get certified immediately, but so you have a recognised structure to point at.
What is an AI impact assessment?
AI impact assessment
An AI impact assessment is a written check, before a high-risk system goes live, of who it affects and whether they can challenge its decision.

An AI impact assessment is a written review, completed before a high-risk AI system goes live, of who it affects and what could go wrong for them. It also asks whether someone wrongly affected has a real way to challenge the decision, not just a right to ask a question.

The EU AI Act calls this a fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27 requires it from deployers that are public-law bodies or private entities delivering a public service. It also applies to any deployer using a high-risk system to score creditworthiness. The same goes for pricing life and health insurance. The assessment has to name the process the system sits inside, how often it runs, and which people or groups it is likely to affect. It has to describe the human oversight in place, and the governance and complaint routes that kick in if a risk shows up. The deployer sends the finished assessment to the national market surveillance authority. Article 27 lets this assessment build on an existing data protection impact assessment rather than repeat it. Where the two overlap, the newer document only has to add what the DPIA does not already answer.

## Why it comes up It comes up wherever an AI system's output changes what a real person is offered - a loan, a job interview, an insurance price, a public benefit. A board hears about it once a pilot nears launch and legal asks who reviewed fairness before customers saw it. Procurement teams increasingly expect a written answer rather than a verbal assurance, since the assessment itself is what a regulator can ask to see. ## What to do about it Name the specific groups the system could disadvantage before launch. Use the actual decision it makes and who it makes it about. Write down the mitigation for each risk identified, and who checked that the mitigation actually works rather than just exists on paper. I flag which systems need this specific assessment inside the [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) before the question comes from a customer's legal team instead of from me.
What is an AI management system?
AI management system
An AI management system is the recurring set of policies, roles and reviews a company runs to govern its AI, not a one-off risk assessment.

An AI management system is the plan-do-check-act cycle a company runs to govern its AI. It sets policy, does the work, checks results, then adjusts and repeats. ISO/IEC 42001 is the standard that certifies a company actually runs the cycle, not just writes it down.

That cycle is what the standard specifies in full, covering policy, risk treatment, resourcing and internal audit for the whole organisation rather than one product. Building to this shape does not require certifying against it. A management system is a way of working; certification is a separate, optional proof of it. The EU AI Act does not require this broader system. Article 17 requires a narrower relative of it instead. Every provider of a high-risk AI system must run a documented quality management system, covering the risk-management process, post-market monitoring and serious-incident procedures among other elements. Its depth scales to the size of the provider's organisation. That overlap is why the two get treated as one project, not two. Building the policy, the register and the review cycle once tends to satisfy the voluntary standard. For a provider of high-risk systems, it also tends to satisfy the legal minimum Article 17 sets.

## Why it comes up A procurement questionnaire increasingly asks for an AI management system by name, not a risk assessment for one product, because a buyer wants proof governance survives a change of staff. A board hears the phrase once a competitor announces ISO/IEC 42001 certification and asks whether the company should follow. The honest answer is usually that the certificate matters less than the structure behind it, since an unread policy is worth little more than none. ## What to do about it Write the policy in one page an engineer would actually follow, not a document written for an auditor. Name an owner for the system as a whole, not just for individual products. Set a fixed date to review the register rather than waiting for a customer to ask. I score exactly this structure against ISO/IEC 42001 in the two-week [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment), so the gap list is evidence rather than a guess.
What is an AI register?
AI register
An AI register is a company's own inventory of every AI system it uses, who owns each one, and how risky it is.
An AI register is a company's own inventory of every AI system it builds, buys or uses, listing what it does, what data it touches, who owns it and how risky it is.

A working entry covers what a system does, what data it can see, which vendor or model sits behind it, who owns it, and a rough risk tier. That applies as much to a vendor tool an ops team subscribed to on a card as to a flagship product. It is the single most requested document in a procurement or investor due-diligence process. Everything else, from a data-flow diagram to a risk assessment, builds on the list it provides. Most companies cannot produce one on short notice, because tools get added by individual teams without a central record. The honest answer to "what AI do you run" is too often "we are not sure." Building a register does not need new software. It forces one decision per system: a named owner. That turns a question a reviewer might spend a day chasing into a document you hand over in a meeting.

## Why it comes up It is usually the first document a procurement team or an investor's checklist asks for, and the first one a company discovers it lacks. A security review cannot get past "what AI systems touch our data" without one. A board asking about AI risk gets a shorter conversation once a real list sits in front of it. The EU AI Act raises the stakes for high-risk systems: Article 71 requires joining a public EU database. ## What to do about it Build a spreadsheet before anything more elaborate: system name, what it does, vendor or model, data it can see, owner, and risk tier, one row per system. Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support instead of relying on a self-reported survey. That is how tools added outside a formal process get missed. Review the list on a fixed schedule, quarterly is reasonable, since a stale register looks worse in review than admitting you lack one.
What is a conformity assessment?
Conformity assessment
A conformity assessment is the check, self-run or done by an outside body, that proves a high-risk AI system meets the EU AI Act before sale.

A conformity assessment is the process a provider completes before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, either checking it internally or having an accredited outside body check it. It shows the system actually meets the EU AI Act's requirements, rather than merely claiming to.

For almost every high-risk system, the outcome is simple: the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off instead. Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standards, the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance, are not fully applied or do not yet exist. The assessment is not a one-time formality. Any substantial change to a system after launch triggers a new one, under whichever route applied the first time. The one exception is a system that keeps learning after deployment. A provider can plan for that drift in advance and record it in the technical documentation before the first assessment. Later changes that stay within that plan do not reopen the process.

## Why it comes up An investor or a board asks how a company knows its AI system is compliant, and a vague assurance is not the same as pointing to a completed assessment and a signed declaration. A procurement team increasingly asks to see evidence the assessment happened at all, rather than taking a compliance claim on trust. It also surfaces at the worst time, during a late-stage system change, when nobody planned for a second assessment. ## What to do about it Work out early, before the system is built, which assessment route applies, since a notified-body review takes far longer to arrange than an internal one and cannot be rushed at launch. Keep the assessment evidence alongside the technical documentation it depends on, not in a file only one person can find. Mapping each system to its likely route is part of the [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) done before a deadline forces the decision.
What is data classification?
Data classification
Data classification is labelling data by sensitivity, such as public, internal or restricted, before deciding what may reach an AI tool.

Data classification means labelling what is in a dataset, document or prompt by sensitivity. Common tiers are public, internal, confidential and restricted. A company can then decide what is allowed to reach a given AI tool. That way nobody pastes something in and finds out the hard way.

NIST's own method for federal systems ties each category to a real question, not a subjective label: what actually happens to confidentiality, integrity or availability if this breaks, meaning who could see this data, alter it, or take it offline? A scheme built the same way works for AI. That is what makes classification useful for a real decision, not a compliance exercise nobody consults. Every additional tool a company adopts multiplies the places a given tier could leak from. That is why the scheme has to live inside the AI register, not beside it. Without one, two employees facing the same document reach different answers. The wrong answer usually only surfaces after the data has already left the building through a chat prompt.

## Why it comes up It is the first practical question underneath any AI acceptable-use policy. Can this go into that tool? Nobody can answer that until someone has labelled what this actually is. A security reviewer asks for the classification scheme by name, not as an abstract principle. The scheme is what turns a policy from a statement of intent into something an employee can actually follow on a Tuesday afternoon. ## What to do about it Keep the scheme small. Three or four tiers is enough for most companies, and a scheme nobody can remember gets ignored the same as none. Map every AI tool in the register to which tiers may reach it. Make the most important rule explicit: customer data and secrets never go into an unclassified tool. The [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) already includes this table, mapped to what may reach a vendor.
What is a DPIA?
A DPIA, or data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR check of privacy risk before high-risk personal-data processing begins.

A DPIA, short for data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR review completed before a company begins personal-data processing likely to carry high privacy risk. It assesses what data is collected, why, and how that risk is being reduced, distinct from a fairness review of the decision itself.

GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default. It has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, that officer must be consulted while the assessment is carried out. Signing off afterward does not count. Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 points the other way too. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

## Why it comes up Almost any AI system worth building processes personal data, which makes a DPIA the default question rather than an edge case, and legal or procurement asks for it specifically once a system moves from a prototype to something touching real customer records. It gets confused with the newer AI Act impact assessment often enough that clarifying the difference is usually the more useful answer than either document alone. ## What to do about it Write the DPIA before the system is built, not after, since a risk found during design is cheap to change and the same risk found after launch usually is not. Start from what is actually being collected and why, not from a template's headings, and consult the data protection officer while there is time to act. The [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lays out the same data classification a DPIA starts from.
What is the EU AI Act?
The EU AI Act is an EU regulation that sorts AI systems into risk tiers and sets legal obligations, heaviest for high-risk systems.
The EU AI Act is an EU regulation, in force since August 2024, that sorts AI systems into risk tiers, from banned practices to high-risk systems, and sets legal obligations that scale with the tier.

Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. Everything else is left largely unregulated. Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there, which is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem. In practice, it changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight, with evidence of both ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a company has, or wants, a customer in the EU, regardless of where it is based. A customer's legal team asks which risk tier your product falls into before they sign, because their own exposure depends on your answer. A board asks about it once a competitor gets fined, or a customer raises it at renewal. The Act follows the AI system's users, not the provider's registered address. ## What to do about it Work out which risk tier each AI system falls into. Most products used inside a normal business are not high-risk, but a few categories, hiring and credit among them, almost always are and deserve a real legal read. For anything near the high-risk category, start the paperwork now: a risk assessment, a named oversight point, and technical documentation. For everything else, keep the register entry current, so the answer is a lookup, not a scramble.
What are evals?
Evals are repeatable tests that score an AI system's output against fixed examples, run before release and after every change.
Evals are repeatable tests that score an AI system's outputs against a fixed set of examples and criteria, run before release and again whenever the prompt, data or model changes.

The comparison that matters is to an ordinary test suite. There is one difference: the system under test can give a different answer each run. A typical eval is a set of inputs with known good answers or a scoring rule. It runs automatically whenever the prompt, the model or the surrounding code changes, with a pass rate tracked over time rather than a single pass or fail. Engineering teams build them because "it worked when I tried it a few times" does not survive a prompt change six months later, once nobody remembers which cases mattered. Security reviewers and boards ask about them because an eval suite is the concrete answer to "how do you know it still works," which otherwise has no answer better than trust. In practice, evals change how a team ships. A prompt or model change runs through the same suite every time, and a drop in the pass rate blocks a release the same way a failing test would.

## Why it comes up A security reviewer or a technical board member asks the same question they would of any release process: what stops a bad change from reaching customers. For a normal codebase, the answer is a test suite. For an AI feature, the honest answer is either an eval suite or "we check by hand." That second answer does not hold up once a product has more than a couple of prompts. ## What to do about it Write down twenty to fifty real cases the system must handle correctly. Draw them from actual support tickets or usage, not invented examples, and include a few you know are hard. Score each case automatically where you can, and by a human reviewer where you cannot. Track the pass rate over time rather than treating one run as final. Run the suite before every prompt or model change ships.
What are guardrails in an AI system?
Guardrails are checks enforced in code around what a model can be asked and what it can say or do, not rules typed into a prompt.

Guardrails are the checks placed around what an AI model can be asked, what it can say, and what it can do. They are enforced in the surrounding code, not left to the model's training. That way an unusual input cannot simply talk the system out of a rule.

In practice a guardrail is one of three things: a topic restriction on what the model will engage with, or an output filter on what a user sees. The third, an action gate, controls what the system may do without a check first. OWASP, an independent security-standards group, publishes its own mitigation list for prompt injection, which reads like a checklist for these three. Privilege control and human approval for high-risk actions are guardrails, not model behaviour. This is closer to what NIST's AI Risk Management Framework calls its Manage function: turning a risk decision into something the system enforces, not something merely written down. Guardrails are how that function shows up in code, not in a policy document nobody checks against production.

## Why it comes up Asking what guardrails a system has is one of the shortest, most common questions in a security review. It is a hard one to answer honestly if the only guardrail is the model's own training and good manners. A board hears it as a proxy for a bigger question: what is the actual worst thing this system could be tricked into doing? And what stands between that action and a real customer? ## What to do about it Write guardrails as rules the code enforces, not text pasted into a prompt. Test each one against an input designed to defeat it, not a well-behaved example. Put a real check in front of any action that spends money, changes a record, or sends something external. That way a failure blocks the action instead of completing it. The [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) builds these checks into the workflow itself, not as a retrofit after an incident.
What is a hallucination rate?
Hallucination rate
A hallucination rate is the share of a model's answers that are confidently wrong, measured against real questions with known correct answers.
A hallucination rate is the share of a model's answers that state something false or invented in the same confident tone as a correct one, measured against questions with known correct answers.

NIST's generative-AI risk guidance calls this failure confabulation, distinct from an ordinary software bug because confidence is never a reliable guide to accuracy here. That makes it different from a crash or an error message, which at least announces itself. A model rarely answers "I don't know": left to guess, it produces a fluent answer instead, which is why the rate has to be measured rather than assumed. Measuring it means running the model against questions with known correct answers. The score is how often the answer is invented rather than true, the same discipline an eval suite already applies to other kinds of failure. That turns a vague worry into a tracked number.

## Why it comes up A board asks this before it asks about model architecture or vendor choice. It turns "is the AI any good" into a number anyone can track quarter to quarter. A company that cannot answer with one, measured on its own real use cases, is really saying "we do not know." That reads differently in a board pack than an honest figure with the method stated plainly. ## What to do about it Measure the rate on the eval suite's real cases, not a generic public benchmark. Behaviour on general trivia says little about a specific product's actual questions. Track the number after every prompt or model change, the way an eval pass rate is tracked. Do not measure it once and assume it holds. The [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this measurement inside continuous integration, so a regression blocks a release.
What makes an AI system high-risk?
High-risk AI system
A high-risk AI system is one the EU AI Act singles out, by product-safety law or by use case such as hiring or credit, for its heaviest duties.

A high-risk AI system is one the EU AI Act classifies as carrying its heaviest legal duties. That happens either because it is a safety component of a regulated product, or because it serves a listed purpose such as hiring, credit scoring or law enforcement. A narrow exemption can apply.

## Why it comes up It is the first question every other AI Act obligation depends on. A customer's legal team or an investor's due diligence checklist asks it before anything else about the system. A board hears it phrased more simply, as "are we in the category that gets the heavy paperwork, and who decided." Getting the classification wrong either way has a real cost, either missed obligations or needless process on a system that never required it. ## What to do about it Run the classification test on each system separately, not on the company as a whole. One product can be high-risk while another, built the same month, is not. Write the decision down, including the reasoning for a not-high-risk conclusion, since an authority can ask to see it later. This classification is exactly what the [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) produces for every system in the inventory, not just the ones already suspected.
What is human-in-the-loop?
Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or can stop an AI system's output before it takes effect, not the system acting alone.
Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or can stop an AI system's output before it takes effect, rather than the system acting on its own once it starts.

The concept sits on a spectrum, from full autonomy at one end to human-on-the-loop at the other, where a person can intervene but does not have to act. Human-in-the-loop sits in between: a person must actively approve each step before it happens. Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. It is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about, for anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and where it still needs one.

## Why it comes up It comes up whenever an AI system's decision touches something real: a loan, a job application, a support case, a medical or safety-adjacent judgement. A customer's legal team wants to know whether a person can catch and correct a bad output before it reaches someone affected. That is not the same as a person being "involved" in some vague sense. A board asks after seeing an automated system make a costly call nobody had reviewed. ## What to do about it Decide, system by system, where full automation is fine, a wrong answer that costs little and is easy to reverse. Decide, too, where a person must review before anything takes effect. Where a person is in the loop, give them enough time and context to catch a bad output. A rubber-stamp screen that exists only to tick a box does not count. Record which category each system falls into in the AI register.
What does human oversight require under the EU AI Act?
Human oversight
Human oversight is the EU AI Act duty that a person assigned to watch a high-risk system can actually understand it and stop it.

Human oversight is the EU AI Act requirement that a person watching a high-risk AI system has the training, time and authority to understand what it is doing and catch a wrong output. It also means the power to stop the system, not just a name on a workflow diagram.

Article 14 splits the mechanism into two kinds of measure. Some are built into the system itself by the provider before it ships. An example is an interface that flags a low-confidence output. Others are measures the provider identifies for the deployer to carry out instead, such as a rule about when a person must review a case before it proceeds. Article 14 spells out five specific capacities the overseeing person needs. They must understand the system's real limits well enough to spot a malfunction, and stay alert to automation bias rather than trusting the output by default. They also need to correctly read what the output actually means, disregard or reverse a specific output when needed, and have a way to halt the system outright.

## Why it comes up It differs from asking whether a human is in the loop. That is a design question about where a person sits in a workflow. Human oversight is a legal test of whether that person is equipped to catch a bad output, with the time, context and authority to stop it. An auditor tests this by asking what the overseer would do in a specific bad case, not whether a review step exists on a diagram. ## What to do about it Name the specific person or role authorised to halt each high-risk system, not a team, and check they have time per case to evaluate output rather than approve on reflex. Train that person specifically on automation bias. A rushed or over-trusting reviewer defeats the requirement even when the process looks correct. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) includes reviewing who watches each system, and whether they could catch a failure this week.
ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international, certifiable standard for the management system a company runs to govern its AI.

ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard that sets out what an AI management system must do. That means the policies an organisation follows to govern its own AI, checked on a cycle rather than written once. It was published in December 2023.

ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence published it in December 2023. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard a company can be audited and certified against by an accredited third party. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask where you sit against it, because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim. In practice, working towards it means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. None of that requires certification itself.

## Why it comes up A procurement team building a vendor shortlist asks for it by name. A board that already understands ISO 27001 reaches for the same mental model, and asks whether an AI equivalent exists. Because it is a certifiable standard, not a public framework, it carries more weight in a formal audit than a self-written policy. That is why a customer's legal team may put it on a checklist before reading what is in it. ## What to do about it Full certification is a real project with an external auditor, and most companies at seed to growth stage do not need it yet. What is worth doing now is running the standard's own structure without the audit: a documented risk-assessment method, an AI system inventory, and a review of that inventory on a fixed schedule. That gives you "built to the same structure, without the certificate," a stronger position than silence or an unsupported claim.
What is an LLM gateway?
LLM gateway
An LLM gateway is a single service every call to a language model passes through, for auth, logging and filtering.
An LLM (large language model) gateway is a single service every model call passes through, so a company can enforce authentication, logging, rate limits and content filtering in one place.

Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. Through that point, a company can control who is allowed to call a model. It can log every prompt and response for an audit trail, and redact sensitive data before it leaves the building. It can also apply rate and cost limits, and fail over to a different provider if one goes down. Without a gateway, API keys end up scattered across a codebase, and nobody holds a full log of what was sent to a vendor. A data leak through a prompt stays invisible until a customer or regulator finds it first. Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. It also gives a direct, specific answer to a vendor questionnaire's question about how model access is controlled. That beats a description of several applications each doing it inconsistently.

## Why it comes up A security questionnaire almost always asks how access to the model provider is controlled and logged. "Each team manages its own API key" is a poor answer. A board or customer asks a version of the same question after a well-publicised leak elsewhere, where a prompt carrying sensitive data reached a third-party model unlogged. Without a gateway, nobody can produce every prompt sent to a vendor last month. ## What to do about it Put one gateway in front of every model call before adding a second application that talks to a model, not after. Route all API keys through it rather than into individual codebases, and log every request and response. Redact anything that looks like a customer identifier or a secret before it leaves. Solid open-source and hosted options already exist, so this is rarely worth building in house.
What is a model card?
Model card
A model card is a short document a model's maker publishes on what it was built for, how it performs, and where not to use it.

A model card is a short, standard-shaped document a model's maker publishes. It describes what the model was built for, and how it performs across groups and conditions. It also names where the model should not be used, closer to a spec sheet than a sales page.

The format comes from a 2018 paper. It proposed model cards as a response to models shipping with no consistent account of how they had actually been tested. A rigorous card reports evaluation broken out by group: race, geographic location, sex, skin type. It also breaks out intersections, such as age combined with race, instead of one blended figure that hides where performance drops. NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a card has most likely skipped the evaluation itself, not just the paperwork describing it.

## Why it comes up Procurement asks a model vendor for it directly once evaluating more than one option. A card makes two vendors comparable on the same axes, rather than on whatever each chose to advertise. A technical due-diligence review reads the limitations section specifically. That is where a vendor is most likely to have been honest about where the model actually struggles. ## What to do about it Ask every model vendor for their card before signing. Read the limitations section before the headline numbers: the numbers are chosen by the vendor, and the limitations rarely are. If a company fine-tunes or wraps a base model itself, write a short card of its own. Describe what changed and what was tested. The vendor questionnaire this request belongs in is one of the four documents in the [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit).
What is model provenance?
Model provenance
Model provenance is a traceable record of what a model was built from - its base model, its training data, and the licence covering both.

Model provenance is a traceable record of what a model is built from. That means which base model it started from, what data trained or fine-tuned it, and what licence covers the result. A buyer needs this to know what it is allowed to do with the output.

Article 53 of the EU AI Act turned this from a private claim into a published one for general-purpose models. Providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, following a template the AI Office issued. That summary covers the scale of the data, and whether it includes licensed material, scraped web content, user data or synthetic data. For a smaller company building on someone else's model, provenance is a due-diligence question, not a publishing duty. Work through it before signing, not after. That distinction decides who actually reads the summary, and when: before a contract is signed, not after a customer's legal team goes looking for where the data came from.

## Why it comes up A customer's legal team asks it once a product's output could plausibly end up in something they publish, resell or use to make a decision. They inherit whatever rights problem the underlying model carries. It also comes up quietly in procurement: which model is actually behind a feature can have a different answer than the vendor's marketing page implies. That gap widens once a vendor swaps providers without telling anyone. ## What to do about it Ask every model vendor what the model was trained on, or where its training-data summary sits if the vendor owes one. Ask what licence covers the weights and output. Record the answer in the AI register next to that system, not in an email thread nobody can find during a review. Reading the actual vendor list, not asking a company to describe it from memory, is what the [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) does.
What is the NIST AI RMF?
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary US framework for managing AI risk across a system's whole lifecycle.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is a voluntary US framework, published by NIST in January 2023, for identifying and managing the risks of an AI system across its design, development and use.

The framework sets out four functions an organisation applies to an AI system. GOVERN covers policy and accountability, while MAP covers understanding context and risk. Testing and metrics fall under MEASURE. Acting on what it found is MANAGE's job. It is not a law, and it is not sector specific. A bank, a hospital and a ten-person startup can all use the same structure. US procurement teams, and increasingly non-US ones, ask about it because it gives a common vocabulary for a question that used to have no fixed answer: how you know an AI system's risks are actually managed, not just discussed once. In practice, adopting it means someone can point to a specific function, and to a specific piece of evidence behind it. That beats a general assurance that everything is under control.

## Why it comes up It comes up in almost every vendor security questionnaire, and in board packs once a company runs more than one AI system. A customer's risk team wants a framework they recognise, not a bespoke description of your process, because it lets them compare you against every other vendor they review. A board wants the same thing for a different reason: a structure to ask questions against, rather than trusting that engineering thought of everything. ## What to do about it Read the four functions once, properly, rather than skimming a summary. Map what you already do against GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, and write down the gaps honestly. You do not need to implement all of it before you can talk about it. A short document listing what you have, your review step, and what you still owe against each function beats a claim of full compliance with nothing behind it.
What is observability for an AI system?
Observability is the ability to see exactly what a live AI system was asked, what it did, and what it answered, for any one case.

Observability is the ability to see, after the fact, exactly what a live AI system was asked. For any one case someone points to, it also shows what the system retrieved or called, and what it answered. An aggregate chart alone cannot explain one specific customer's bad experience.

For an agentic workflow, a system that also calls tools to look things up or take actions on its own, the record has to extend further. It needs every tool call made along the way, and what each one returned, not just the final input and output. A wrong outcome usually traces back to one step in a longer chain. Skipping tool-call logging leaves exactly that step unrecorded. This differs from a simple uptime dashboard. It can show a system is running while saying nothing about whether one specific answer, given to one specific person, was actually right. NIST's risk management framework calls this its Measure function: a system only counts as measured if it keeps being tested and tracked after release, not just before.

## Why it comes up A customer or an internal investigation asks: show me exactly what happened in this one case. A system with only aggregate metrics cannot answer. That is precisely the gap a security review is testing for when it asks about monitoring. It also comes up after a customer complaint that a specific answer was wrong. The honest response depends entirely on whether that exact exchange was ever recorded. ## What to do about it Log the full input, every step the system took including tool calls, and the output for every real request, not a sample. Keep those logs long enough to support an investigation. Make sure any one case can be pulled up by its own reference, rather than only appearing inside an average. This logging, plus a cost-per-outcome view, ships from the first release in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).
What is post-market monitoring under the EU AI Act?
Post-market monitoring
Post-market monitoring is the EU AI Act duty to keep collecting real-world data on a high-risk system after it ships, not just before.

Post-market monitoring is the EU AI Act duty on a provider to keep collecting and analysing real-world performance data on a high-risk AI system for as long as it is in use. Problems that appear after launch get caught this way, rather than assumed away by the original testing.

Article 72 requires a documented monitoring system, sized to the technology and the risk of the specific system. It has to actively and systematically collect and analyse data on how the system performs once it is actually in use. Deployers feed into it directly, since Article 26 requires them to monitor the system on their end and report back to the provider. That way, the provider is not relying on its own visibility alone. The monitoring plan is not a separate document. Article 72 makes it part of the system's technical documentation, built and updated alongside it, not bolted on after a complaint. A pattern the monitoring turns up is also the raw material for the next duty in the chain: deciding whether what happened counts as a serious incident that has to be reported.

## Why it comes up Does anyone keep watching this system, or was it tested once and left alone? That is the specific question a customer's security team or a regulator asks after any AI failure story in the press. A board hears it as reassurance that a problem would surface through a defined process rather than a customer complaint reaching the news first. Providers who can only describe pre-launch testing, and nothing after, usually have no answer. ## What to do about it Write the monitoring plan before launch - what gets measured, who reviews it, how often - since a plan invented after a problem appears is not the same thing. Build a route for deployer-reported issues to reach the provider. A monitoring system that never hears from the people using it day to day is monitoring very little. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) I run keeps this review on a fixed schedule, not only when a customer complains.
What is prompt injection?
Prompt injection
Prompt injection is text, typed directly or hidden in a document a model reads, that gets the model to follow it as an instruction.

Prompt injection is text that gets a model to treat it as an instruction rather than content. It can be typed by a user, or hidden inside a document, webpage or email the model reads. OWASP, a security-standards group, ranks it as the top risk for large language model applications.

Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text. It has kept that position through every edition of the list, most recently the 2026 revision. The reason is structural: the model reads instructions and untrusted data through the same channel. A filter tuned on known patterns still misses a novel phrasing. Every mitigation available today reduces the odds of a successful attack; none removes them.

## Why it comes up It is the first thing a security reviewer probes on any AI feature that reads outside content. That means a webpage, an uploaded file, an email, or a customer's own message history. The concern is not academic. A model that can also send an email, issue a refund or query a database turns a successful injection into something already done. It is no longer just an embarrassing reply. ## What to do about it Never let a model's output directly trigger a sensitive action without a check enforced in code. Keep the model's own permissions to the smallest set it needs. Treat anything the model reads from outside the conversation as untrusted input, the way a web application treats a user-supplied string. Evals for exactly this kind of attack belong in the same pipeline that gates every other change. That is how I structure the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).
What is the difference between a provider and a deployer?
Provider vs deployer
Provider and deployer are EU AI Act roles - a provider builds or brands a system, a deployer uses it, and the two owe different duties.
Provider vs deployer is the EU AI Act split between the company that builds an AI system and the company that runs it. Most of the Act's paperwork depends on which of the two roles a company holds.

Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. Giving the system away under your own brand still makes you the provider. A deployer is defined by use, not branding: using the system under the deployer's own authority. The only carve-out is personal, non-professional activity. A company using a tool internally is a deployer even if it never touches a customer. That test has a sharp edge. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the company actually wrote.

## Why it comes up It surfaces in a contract negotiation once both sides realise the label matters more than expected, because a provider owes technical documentation and a conformity assessment while a deployer mainly owes human oversight and monitoring. A board hears about it when a vendor's contract quietly assigns the company duties it assumed the vendor carried. Getting the role wrong can leave a company holding an obligation nobody budgeted for. ## What to do about it Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company, since rebranding one vendor's model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. Write the answer into the AI register alongside the risk tier, since a security questionnaire will eventually ask for both. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I answer this kind of question inside a live negotiation.
What is red teaming for an AI system?
Red teaming
Red teaming is deliberately trying to break an AI system the way an attacker would, before they do, to find the failure nobody tested.

Red teaming means deliberately trying to break an AI system, the way a motivated attacker or a determined bad-faith user would, before they actually do. It aims at finding the failure nobody wrote a test case for, not at confirming cases already known to work.

A red team engagement produces a different kind of output than a test run. It is a list of the specific techniques that worked, detailed enough for someone else to reproduce the failure. It also carries a judgement on what an attacker could actually do with it. That reproducibility is what separates a report from an anecdote about something that broke once. NIST's generative AI profile recommends red teaming as a check against specific categories of harm, including information leakage and harmful content generation. Those failures depend on someone actively trying to cause them; they rarely show up in ordinary use. The finding that matters is the one nobody predicted going in.

## Why it comes up Boards and security reviewers increasingly ask for it by name, rather than accepting "we ran evals" as a full answer. An eval suite built by the same team that built the system tends to test what that team already expected to go wrong. It matters more, not less, once a system can take actions or read outside content. A missed failure then moves from a bad reply to a completed action. ## What to do about it Budget real time, not an afternoon, for someone to actively try prompt injection, data extraction and off-limits requests. Do it against the actual live system, not a sanitised demo. Write down exactly what broke, and fix the underlying guardrail, not just the one example that happened to get tried. I treat this as part of shipping in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint), folding findings back into the eval suite before launch.
What is retrieval augmented generation?
Retrieval augmented generation
Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, has a model look up relevant passages at answer time instead of relying only on its training.

Retrieval augmented generation, shortened to RAG, is an architecture where a model looks up relevant passages from a document store at answer time. It reads them alongside the question. This means an answer can cite a current document, rather than relying only on training data.

The document store is usually a vector index. Passages are converted into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and a query is matched against them by similarity, not exact keyword. That is what lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document. OWASP, the group that publishes widely used security-risk lists, tracks this as its own risk category. In a shared vector database, one customer's data can leak into another customer's results. Embeddings themselves can sometimes be inverted, too, to recover the source text they were built from. Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

## Why it comes up Procurement asks "is this RAG, or did you train on our data," because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer's content into the model's own weights. It also comes up once accuracy is questioned. A wrong answer usually traces to a retrieval problem, not a flaw in the model itself. ## What to do about it Control access at the document-store level, not only at the chat interface. RAG will surface anything in the index to anyone who can ask the right question, regardless of who is meant to see it. Treat the document store itself as a data-classification boundary. Check what happens when a document containing hidden instructions ends up inside it. That exact scenario is one of the checks in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).
What counts as a serious incident under the EU AI Act?
Serious incident reporting
Serious incident reporting is the EU AI Act duty to tell a regulator, fast, when a high-risk system causes real harm or a rights breach.

Serious incident reporting is the EU AI Act duty to notify the relevant national authority after a high-risk AI system causes serious harm. It falls on the provider, the company that built the system, and sometimes the deployer, the company running it. The clock is tight and legally fixed.

The duty falls on the provider, the company that built the system, and sometimes on the deployer, the company running it. It applies once a malfunction leads to death, serious harm, or a serious breach of someone's fundamental rights. Article 73 fixes the clock in days, not in vague urgency. The default is fifteen days from when the provider becomes aware of the incident. A widespread infringement or a serious disruption to critical infrastructure tightens that to two days. A death tightens it further, to ten days. Every deadline runs from awareness, not from the incident itself. Once the report is filed, the provider has to investigate: assess the risk, take corrective action, and cooperate with the authority. It cannot alter the system in a way that would affect the investigation's findings without telling the authority first. The duty also covers serious harm to property or the environment, not only harm to people, though that case still runs on the fifteen-day default.

## Why it comes up It surprises companies who assume that deploying a high-risk system is a one-time compliance exercise, the same way a data-breach notification law surprises a company that has never had to report one before. A board's real question is usually simpler - if something goes badly wrong, does the company already know who calls the regulator, or would that decision be made live, under pressure, by whoever happens to be in the room. ## What to do about it Decide in advance, in writing, who has the authority to judge that an incident is serious enough to report, rather than leaving that call to whoever notices the problem first. Preserve the system's state at the time of the incident for investigation, instead of immediately patching it away. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) makes me the named point of contact for this kind of question, answered before it is urgent.
What is shadow AI?
Shadow AI
Shadow AI is any AI tool staff use for company work without IT or security's knowledge, from an app to a browser extension.
Shadow AI is any AI tool an employee uses for company work without IT or security's knowledge. Examples range from a personal chatbot account to a browser extension or a locally run model.

The hardest form to spot is a model downloaded and run locally on a laptop. It never crosses the network as a request to a known AI vendor. The same problem shows up wherever an employee reaches for a tool without asking. A developer might call a model's API directly from a side project. A browser extension might quietly send page content to a third party to generate its summary. None of it sits inside a contract governing how that vendor handles company or customer data, because no one negotiated one. None of it appears in the AI register either. A security review or an incident response then starts from a blind spot, not a known list. The tool itself is rarely the real risk. The missing record of its use is.

## Why it comes up It is usually the first uncomfortable finding of a readiness assessment, and nobody did anything malicious. The register a company thought was complete turns out to have gaps. That happens the moment someone checks browser extensions and expense reports, instead of asking teams to self-report. A customer's security team asks about it, having been burned before. A board hears one checkable question: could an employee be pasting customer data into a public tool right now? ## What to do about it Look rather than ask: check browser extension inventories, expense reports for AI subscriptions, and API billing for model providers nobody remembers approving. Publish a short list of approved tools, and a fast route to request a new one. The main driver of shadow AI is an approval process slower than the problem it solves. Fold anything found straight into the AI register, rather than treating discovery and governance as separate steps.
What is a sub-processor?
A sub-processor is a vendor an AI provider uses behind the scenes to handle a company's data, and GDPR requires permission before it does.

A sub-processor is a vendor an AI provider hands a company's data to behind the scenes. The model provider behind a SaaS tool is a common example. GDPR Article 28 requires the provider to get the customer's permission, and to bind the sub-processor to the same data protections by contract.

GDPR Article 28 calls the AI vendor the processor and your company the controller. It gives the processor two ways to bring a sub-processor in. Specific authorisation names the sub-processor up front, so the controller signs off by name. General authorisation lets the processor add sub-processors as needed, but it has to tell the controller first and give a real chance to object. Either way, the processor must pass down the same data-protection obligations it owes directly, in the contract itself, not just a notice. The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops sit between a company's data and the last party that can actually see it.

## Why it comes up It is a routine line on a security questionnaire: "list your sub-processors." It is also a revealing one. Most AI features are built on someone else's model, which makes a sub-processor almost guaranteed rather than an edge case. A buyer who skips the question is signing a contract blind. They will not know where their data actually goes once it leaves the vendor's own systems. ## What to do about it Ask every AI vendor for its sub-processor list, and how it notifies customers of a change. Then check honestly: does the notice give a real chance to object, or just a record that it happened? Fold the answer into the AI register entry for that vendor, next to the data classification of what reaches them. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I check vendor contracts for this gap before a renewal.
What is technical documentation under the EU AI Act?
Technical documentation
Technical documentation is the dossier a provider keeps on a high-risk AI system - its purpose, design, data, performance and monitoring plan.

Technical documentation is the dossier a provider of a high-risk AI system must keep. It covers purpose, design logic, training data, performance metrics, risk process and monitoring plan. It has to be clear enough that a regulator can assess it without the original engineers in the room.

The EU AI Act sets the content directly in Annex IV, rather than leaving it to the provider's judgement. A national authority or notified body has to be able to assess it without relying on the provider's own explanation. Article 11 lets a small or micro enterprise use a simplified version of the same form, one the Commission publishes for that purpose. Article 18 sets how long it has to survive: ten years from when the system was placed on the market or put into service. A national competent authority can request it at any point in that window. The same retention duty covers the quality management system records and the EU declaration of conformity too, not the technical documentation alone.

## Why it comes up It is different from a marketing spec sheet or an engineering wiki page, and a regulator or notified body wants the specific content the Act lists, not a general description of the product. It also comes up in procurement due diligence, where a buyer of a high-risk system sometimes asks to see excerpts before signing. A vendor who can produce none of it has told you something. ## What to do about it Start the document on the first day of build, recording design decisions as they are made, since reconstructing the reasoning behind a choice months later is far harder than writing it down at the time. Version it alongside the system itself, so the documentation for a given release actually matches what shipped. The register and policy shape this documentation builds on sits in the [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) ahead of the deeper regulatory detail.
What actually belongs in an AI acceptable use policy
What a working AI acceptable use policy has to decide, what it must refuse to do, and how a company of 30 to 300 people gets staff to follow it.

An AI acceptable use policy for a company of 30 to 300 people classifies which data may reach which AI vendor, names who approves a new tool, and requires review before AI output reaches a customer. It must not try to ban AI outright or list every tool by name. It also names who decides after a breach.
A policy earns compliance when it names an owner, a data tier and a request path for a new tool, not when it lists every AI product by name.

The EU AI Act already requires disclosure once an AI system talks to a customer directly or generates content someone could mistake for work a human did, regardless of whether the system counts as high-risk.
Banning AI outright does not remove the risk. It moves the same activity out of sight, which is how shadow AI starts.
A rule with nobody named to decide what happens after a breach is a suggestion, and staff work that out within days.
ISO/IEC 42001 treats the policy as part of a recurring cycle: owned, reviewed on a schedule, and checked against what the AI register actually shows people using.
Does a company of 30 people really need a written AI policy?

Yes. Once more than one person can install a browser extension or open a chatbot account, verbal guidance stops being enough. A one-page policy with a named owner is less work than the meeting that follows the first incident.
Should the policy list every approved AI tool by name?

No. A named-tool list goes stale within weeks and implies anything missing from it is fine by default. Classify data instead, and give staff a fast path to add a tool, so the approved list stays current without a rewrite.
Who should own the policy?

One named person with the authority to approve or block a tool, and the standing to answer for that decision. That is usually whoever already owns AI risk generally, not a committee and not an HR document nobody maintains.
What happens the first time someone breaks the policy?

It depends on intent. Someone who used an unapproved tool without knowing the rule gets a conversation and a correction. Someone who ignored a direct no, or hid that AI wrote something they signed their own name to, goes through the same disciplinary process as any other policy breach.
