How is this different from a data protection or security policy?

It sits next to them, not instead of them. A security policy controls access and infrastructure. A data protection policy covers personal data generally. This one is specific to what staff paste into an AI system and what a vendor may do with it.

Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong, in language a new hire reads in one sitting. ## What does a working AI acceptable use policy actually need to say? A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Six sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent. | Section | What it decides | Failure it prevents | | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope | Which staff, contractors and AI tools the policy covers. | A contractor or a new hire assuming the rules do not apply to them. | | Data classification | Which data tier may reach which category of AI vendor. | Client or personal data pasted into a public chatbot with no data agreement. | | Approved tools and requests | Which AI systems are pre-approved, and how staff add another one. | Staff picking an unapproved tool because asking takes too long. | | Human review | Whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer, a contract or a filing. | An unreviewed AI draft going out under someone's name. | | Customer disclosure | When a customer must be told they are talking to an AI system or seeing AI-made content. | A hidden AI interaction reaching a customer where disclosure is a legal duty. | | Vendor training use | Whether a vendor may use company or client input to train its own models. | Confidential input quietly improving a vendor's public model. | | Ownership and review | Who owns the policy, and how often it is checked against what staff actually use. | A policy that describes a tool nobody uses, and stays silent about the one everyone does. | | Incident reporting | What staff do the moment an AI system produces something wrong or exposes data. | A bad output or a leak going unreported because nobody knew who to tell. | | Enforcement | What happens after a breach, and who decides. | A rule everyone knows is never actually enforced. | The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system. It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships, not leave it to whoever built the feature to remember. ## What should the policy refuse to try to do? A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice: once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser, and once because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support. Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day it is published and is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, which is the opposite of what a reviewer wants to see. An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern. ## What do you do about the tools staff are already using? By the time a policy is drafted, some staff are already drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account, running a browser extension nobody vetted, or building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves, without asking anyone first. That is [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai), and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make. Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running, which beats trusting a self-reported survey. ## What happens when someone breaks the policy? Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client's contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one. One named role decides what happens next: the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened, decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it, and choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems. That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy does not need a punishment system of its own; it needs a clear point where that existing process starts. Silence is its own answer too: a policy that never states what happens after a breach gets tested once, and staff learn from the result whether any of it is real. ## Who should own it, and how does it stay current? The same person who is already accountable for AI risk generally should hold this document, for the reason a shared inbox cannot hold it: someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory. A review interval only works if it is tied to something that actually changes: a new hire, a new vendor account, a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it. The version I run for my own practice is public at [my AI policy](/ai-policy), one page, as a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The [Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) sets out the same structure as a table you can copy, sized for a company with more than one person to coordinate. ## What doesn't a policy like this solve? A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, that gap usually surfaces during an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) before it ever reaches the policy stage, because there is no obvious person to hand the draft to. Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. What it removes is the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway. Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.
Evals in CI for LLM agents, without a golden answer
How to build an eval set from production traffic, score an LLM agent without a golden answer, and fail a merge in CI when it regresses.

Evals in CI run a fixed test set on every change. A regression then fails the build, the way a broken unit test does. Most agent tasks have no single right answer. Score with a rubric-based judge, a groundedness check, or a comparison against the last good version. Track the pass rate over time.

Evals in CI put a fixed test set on every prompt, model, or code change. The build fails when the pass rate drops. A regression gets caught before a reviewer approves the pull request, not after a customer notices. Build the set from real production traffic. Sample across a period long enough that one quiet week does not flatter the result. Most agent tasks have no single correct answer. Score them in layers instead. Start with deterministic checks: a tool call shape, a required field, a data format. Add a reference-free judge for whether an answer is grounded in what the agent retrieved. Fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version for everything else. Treat the judge as a component that needs calibration against a human-labelled sample, not as ground truth. A cost ceiling per completed run sits in the same job as the score. An expensive change then fails the build for the same reason a wrong one does.
Build the eval set from real production traffic sampled across a window long enough that a quiet period does not flatter the result.
Score agentic tasks in layers: deterministic checks for anything mechanical, a reference-free judge for groundedness, and a comparison against the last known-good version for everything else.
Calibrate the judge against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule, and let it skip a case rather than force a score it cannot support.
Put a cost ceiling per completed run in the same job as the quality score, so an expensive change fails the build for the same reason a wrong one does.
A failing check blocks the merge by default; only a named reviewer can override it, and every override is logged next to the run it overrode.
How many cases does an eval set need before it is useful in CI?

Fewer than most teams assume. A few dozen real, representative cases that cover the failure modes support has already seen catch most regressions, and a large synthetic set with no connection to real traffic often catches less. Add a case the day a bug reaches production, and the set keeps pace with how the agent is actually used, rather than how it was imagined at launch.
Can an eval set built from old tickets go stale?

Yes, in two ways. The product changes and old cases stop representing real traffic, or a case with a wrong or outdated expected answer starts failing runs that are actually correct. Review the set on a fixed schedule, retire cases the product has outgrown, and pull in new ones from whatever just broke.
Should a flaky eval block a merge the same way a clear regression does?

No. A check that disagrees with itself run to run is broken, not informative, and forcing it to gate a build just adds noise to the release process. Quarantine it: leave it running and visible, stop it from blocking anything, and assign someone to fix its rubric or its sampling before it rejoins the checks that actually gate a merge.
Does the judge need to be a stronger model than the one being tested?

Not necessarily, but many teams find a stronger judge catches subtler failures than a same-tier one, since judging is its own hard task. Weigh that against cost: the judge runs on every case in the set, every time the pipeline runs, and a large judge model on a large eval set is usually where the cost ceiling gets tested first.

An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one. A model provider's silent update slips through every time. Putting [an eval suite](/glossary/evals) in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching. ## How do you build an eval set from production traffic? Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent's eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is. Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. On only.help, my own product, the support-triage rollout built its first eval set from tickets already answered. It then found that the [first week looked better than the system really was](/case-studies/only-help-agentic-support), purely from seasonal timing. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects. That mix is a sturdier base than one convenient week. Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code that it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request. Change it through the same review a code change gets. Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how the agent is actually used. ## How do you score an agent when there is no golden answer? Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first. Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs. OWASP's list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed. It should also check that the tool fires correctly when needed. For the answer's content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is simply not supported by anything the system looked at. That is the failure mode a plain accuracy score misses entirely. Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor. NIST's AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute. ## What happens when the judge itself is flaky? A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge's own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage. Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of surfacing it. Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet. When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build. ## What should the pipeline check, and what does a failing check do to the build? Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails. | What to score | How to score it | What a failing score does to the build | | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Task success on labelled cases | Exact match or a deterministic rule against a known-good answer. | Blocks the merge immediately, with no override. | | Task success with no golden answer | A rubric-based judge scores the answer against stated criteria, not against a reference. | Blocks the merge once the pass rate drops below the floor set for that task. | | Faithfulness to retrieved context | A reference-free judge checks whether each claim traces back to a document the agent actually retrieved. | Blocks the merge; an unsupported claim counts as a defect, not a style note. | | Preference against the last good version | Pairwise comparison: the judge sees both outputs, blind to which is new, and picks a winner. | Blocks the merge if the new version loses on more cases than the agreed margin allows. | | Tool-call correctness | Deterministic check that the agent called the right tool with a valid, schema-checked argument set. | Blocks the merge; a malformed call fails loudly instead of degrading quietly. | | Judge-human agreement | Re-run the rubric against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule and compare agreement. | Does not block a single pull request; a drop pages the eval owner to fix the rubric. | | Cost per completed run | Sum of model and tool cost across the eval set, divided by cases completed. | Blocks the merge once the run exceeds the ceiling set in the pipeline config. | | Response time under load | Wall-clock time per case, measured in the same job as the scores. | Warns on the pull request; blocks only if it breaches the budget agreed with the product owner. | ## Where does the cost ceiling sit? Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it. Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression. That holds even if every other score stays green. A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice. ## What does the pipeline do when a check fails? A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log. Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget can page an owner instead. So can a drop in judge-human agreement, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone's memory of which checks are actually load-bearing. Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.
How to build an AI system register in a week
A step-by-step way to build an AI system register in a week without buying a tool, so a security reviewer gets the document they ask for first.

An AI system register lists every AI tool a company builds, buys or lets a team adopt: what it does, what data it touches, who owns it, and how risky it is. A security reviewer asks for this list before anything else. A team builds a usable version in a week with a spreadsheet and five interviews, no software required.

A security reviewer asks for an AI system register before model choice, prompt design or accuracy come up. It is the inventory of every AI system in use, however it got there. Each entry records what it does, what data reaches it, which vendor sits behind it, who owns it, and how risky it is. Every later question a reviewer asks only makes sense once that list exists. Most companies of thirty to three hundred people do not have one, not because the work is hard, but because nobody was ever assigned to write it down. Building the first version does not need a tool or a budget line. It needs a spreadsheet, a short interview with each team that touches a model, and one person who agrees to keep the list current once the interviews stop.
An AI system register is the document a security reviewer asks for before anything else, because every later question about data, contracts or incidents depends on already knowing what runs.
A usable register lists what each system does, what data it touches, which vendor sits behind it, who owns it internally and a rough risk tier, one row per system.
The fastest way to build the first version is a spreadsheet and direct interviews with engineering, marketing, finance and support, not a survey people can quietly skip.
A register nobody updates gets treated the same as no register in a review, so it needs one named owner and a fixed date to recheck every row.
Do you need a register if your company only uses ChatGPT and a few SaaS tools with AI features?

Yes. A register is not only for models a company builds. It should list any AI feature that can see company or customer data, including a tool a team subscribed to on its own, because that is exactly the kind of system a reviewer or an incident finds first.
How is an AI system register different from a data flow diagram or a risk assessment?

The register comes first. A data flow diagram maps how data moves through one system in detail, and a risk assessment scores how risky a system is, but both need the list of systems, owners and data that the register provides before that work can start. Skip the register and the same discovery gets repeated every time someone asks.
Does an internal register satisfy the registration duty under the EU AI Act?

No. An internal register is a record a company keeps for itself. The public registration duty under Article 49 of the EU AI Act applies separately, only to certain high-risk systems, and is filed in the database the Commission set up under Article 71. Building the internal register first is still the fastest way to find out which systems might owe that separate duty.
Who should own the register after the first week?

A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An AI system register is the fix: one document listing every AI system a company runs, who owns it, and how risky it is. ## What is an AI system register? An AI system register is the full inventory of every AI system a company runs, regardless of how it got there. That includes a customer-facing feature, an internal copilot, or a marketing tool with a model switched on inside it that nobody called an AI project when they signed up. A working entry names what the system does, what data can reach it, which vendor or model sits behind it, who owns it, and a rough risk tier. Some call this same list an [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) rather than an AI system register. Most of the systems on it never started as a formal AI project, which is why the list has to go looking for them rather than wait to be told. ## Why does a security reviewer ask for it before anything else? A security or procurement reviewer asks one version of the same question first: what touches our data. Without a register, answering that means paging engineering, marketing, finance and support one by one, and hoping nobody forgot a tool. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry. Everything a reviewer asks next, a data flow diagram, a vendor contract clause, an incident plan, gets scoped against rows already on this list. Skip the register, and the reviewer either stalls the process or signs off on a system nobody can fully describe. ## What should the register record? A register only earns its keep if a reviewer can answer their own questions from it, without a follow-up meeting. What follows is close to the version I hand a client: enough fields to answer a first review, and no field that exists only to look thorough. | What to record | Why a reviewer wants it | Who fills it and what it does. | A reviewer cannot scope a check against a system they cannot picture. | The system's product or engineering owner. | | Note whether it was built in-house or bought, and which checked. | A register that has not moved in a year gets treated the same as no register at all. | Whoever owns the register process, on a fixed schedule. | ## How do you build one in a week without buying a tool? None of this needs procurement. A spreadsheet, a shared document and five short conversations get a usable first version out the door. - **Monday.** Create the spreadsheet with those three columns, and seed it with every system already in use: the model inside the product, the support tool, the analytics dashboard that quietly added an AI summary. - **Tuesday and Wednesday.** Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support directly, not by survey. Ask each team what they actually use day to day, since a spreadsheet plug-in with a model behind it belongs on the list too. - **Thursday.** Fill in the vendor, data and risk-tier columns from what you heard, and flag anything nobody could describe clearly for a follow-up conversation rather than a guess. - **Friday.** Assign an owner to every row, pick a reviewer for the risk tiers, and put a recheck date on the calendar before anyone calls the list finished. ## What a register does not do Building the register is the easy part of this, and several harder parts of AI governance sit outside it. It does not replace a lawyer's read of a vendor contract. The register tells legal which vendor to check and what data reaches them. It says nothing about whether that vendor's specific contract terms are safe to sign, and those terms change often enough that last year's answer will not do. The registration duty in the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that separate duty; it is not a substitute for filing it. It does not stay accurate on its own, either. Pick one outcome the business already tracks, such as resolved tickets per hour or hours saved on a task, and set a floor for it before the pilot starts. Wire an automatic eval into the build so a prompt or model change that drops the number blocks the release rather than reaching users.

A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs: a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. They also lack a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does. ## Where do pilots actually stop? ### Nobody owns the risk Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator. Ownership is not a shared inbox or a Slack channel. It is one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it. ### Legal has not said which data may leave Most pilots reach a vendor's API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes. The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet. ### There is no measurable outcome A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move, such as tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task. Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly. ### Nobody would notice a regression Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider's own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships, so a regression surfaces first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build. That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. It is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off. ## What has to be true to ship? Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic; most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own. | Condition | What it means in practice | What its absence looks like | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | An owner. | One named person, on the team that runs the system, with authority to pause it. | No one can explain a bad output, so the stall becomes permanent. | | A data classification. | A written answer, agreed with whoever owns data risk, on what a vendor may store. | Every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. | | A measurable outcome. | One number the business already tracks, with a floor the system must clear. | Nobody can prove the pilot works, so it runs quietly forever instead of shipping or dying. | | Evals in CI. | Real test cases run on every prompt or model change; OWASP treats this as baseline hygiene. | A regression reaches a customer before anyone on the team sees it. | | Tracing and cost per outcome. | Every run logged well enough to reconstruct, with a cost a finance team can read. | Nobody can say what a run costs, or which step produced a bad answer. | | Rollback. | A rehearsed way to revert to the last prompt, model or version within minutes. | The team improvises during the first real incident instead of using a tested path. | For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses: a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover. ## How would I sequence it? I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it. ### Pick one process Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An AI readiness and risk assessment is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo that names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move. ### Build it in ninety days A 90-Day Production Sprint turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one, and the rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident. ### Hand it to someone who was in the room The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge. ## What this does not solve This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it. Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence's. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor is allowed to see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you. It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask; it does not answer whether a specific vendor's terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms. The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test, not every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down, which is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do. It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days; it does not shortcut them.

What actually belongs in an AI acceptable use policy — meshin.co

An AI acceptable use policy only earns its place once it decides who approves a new AI tool and which data tier may reach which category of vendor. It also decides whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer or a contract, and when a customer must be told they are dealing with an AI system. Most templates answer the first two questions and stay quiet on the rest. That is exactly why staff read them once and then ignore them. A policy this size needs one named owner, not a committee, and a review interval short enough to catch the tool people started using without asking. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, not a standalone document. The EU AI Act already requires disclosure once an AI system talks to a customer directly. Skip the enforcement clause and none of the rest holds.
Published 8 September 2026 · Updated 8 September 2026

Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong, in language a new hire reads in one sitting.

A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Six sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent.

The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system.

It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships, not leave it to whoever built the feature to remember.

A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice: once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser, and once because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support.

Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day it is published and is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, which is the opposite of what a reviewer wants to see.

An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern.

By the time a policy is drafted, some staff are already drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account, running a browser extension nobody vetted, or building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves, without asking anyone first. That is shadow AI, and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make.

Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running, which beats trusting a self-reported survey.

Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client’s contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one.

One named role decides what happens next: the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened, decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it, and choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems.

That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy does not need a punishment system of its own; it needs a clear point where that existing process starts. Silence is its own answer too: a policy that never states what happens after a breach gets tested once, and staff learn from the result whether any of it is real.

The same person who is already accountable for AI risk generally should hold this document, for the reason a shared inbox cannot hold it: someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory.

A review interval only works if it is tied to something that actually changes: a new hire, a new vendor account, a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it.

The version I run for my own practice is public at my AI policy, one page, as a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The Starter Kit sets out the same structure as a table you can copy, sized for a company with more than one person to coordinate.

A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, that gap usually surfaces during an AI readiness and risk assessment before it ever reaches the policy stage, because there is no obvious person to hand the draft to.

Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. What it removes is the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway.
Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.

Agentic architecture — meshin.co

An agent demo is easy and an agent in production is not, and the gap between them is almost never about the model. It is about the same engineering discipline any other system needs, applied to a component whose output is not deterministic.

Start with evaluation, before the prompt. If you cannot say what a good answer looks like on a set of real cases, you cannot tell whether a change made the system better or simply different. Build the eval set from work that has already been done by people, so there is a known-good answer to compare against, and sample it across a long enough window that seasonality does not flatter you.

Put that eval run in continuous integration. This is the single change that most often turns a prototype into something a team will let near a customer, because it moves the question from an argument about vibes to a number that blocks a merge. A regression should fail the build, in the same job, with the same authority as a broken unit test.

Instrument every call. When an answer is wrong you want to see which retrieval returned which document and what the model was given, not reconstruct it from memory. Tracing turns a support escalation into a quick check instead of a day of guessing.

Set a cost ceiling per outcome and check it in the same job as the evals. A loop that retries three times on a bad tool response is fine in a demo and ruinous at volume. If you cannot state the cost of one completed task, you do not yet know whether the system makes sense.

Then design the boundary. Tool interfaces are where agents actually break, which is why an explicit protocol between the model and your systems is worth adopting, rather than one improvised inside a prompt. Keep the tools narrow, validate their inputs, and make every destructive action reversible.
Finally, keep a rollback path. A prompt is a deployment. Version it, ship it behind the same controls as code, and be able to put yesterday back quickly.
AI for boards — meshin.co

A board does not need a member who can explain how a model works. It needs to know who inside the company is answerable when one gets something wrong in front of a customer, and whether that answer would survive being read back in a dispute. Ask that question at every review, not just the first one.

Ask for three things, by name rather than by department. Who owns AI risk, specifically, not which team owns it. A register of every AI system in use, kept current rather than produced once for an audit. And the last time a customer or a regulator asked a question about this, with the answer that was actually given. Anything less than a name is not an answer.

Do not ask for a demo. A demo proves a model can perform once, in front of people who want it to succeed, which is the least useful thing a board can learn. Do not ask for a token count, a model name, or a list of pilots. Those measure activity, not risk, and a company can produce an impressive slide about all three without anyone being accountable for one of them.

The exposure that actually matters shows up after something goes wrong, not before. A regulator or an insurer will not ask whether the model was good. They will ask whether someone reviewed the system before it reached a customer, whether that review is written down, and whether the questionnaire answer was still true afterwards. A board that has not asked those questions is the one that gets asked them first.

A company of 30 to 300 people needs one named owner, one page of decisions, and the discipline to update both when something changes. A board does this well by asking the same few questions until the answers stop moving.
AI governance — meshin.co

Governance has a bad name in small companies because most of what is sold under that name is written for a bank. A three hundred person company does not need a committee, a maturity model or a consultant to run a workshop. It needs four things that fit on a shared drive and get updated when something changes.

The first is a register: every AI system in use, who owns it, what data reaches it, and whether a person checks its output before a customer sees it. Companies usually find more AI in the building than they expected, because someone signed up for a tool with a credit card and nobody wrote it down.

The second is an acceptable-use policy short enough that people read it. One page. What you may paste into a chat window, what you may not, and who to ask when the answer is unclear. A policy that requires a training course to understand is a policy that gets ignored by the people whose behaviour it was written to change.

The third is a data classification table. Three or four tiers, each with a rule about which vendors may see that tier. This is the document that answers most of a customer security questionnaire, and it is the one companies most often skip because it requires a decision rather than a description.

The fourth is a named owner: one person whose job description says they own AI risk and who has the authority to stop a launch. Frameworks like ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework both assume this person exists. Without them, every answer in a questionnaire is a guess, and every incident becomes a search for who should have been watching.

That is the whole set. It takes about two weeks to produce honestly, and the honest version is worth more than a thorough version that describes a company you are not. When a customer asks who owns AI risk, or a board asks what happens if a model leaks a document, you want to answer from a document that was true last week, not from one that was impressive last year.
AI operating model — meshin.co

Most stalled AI programmes are not blocked on technology. They are blocked because nobody can say who decides whether a system is allowed to touch customer data, and nobody owns the outcome once the pilot team moves on.

An operating model answers three questions. Who chooses which processes get automated. Who reviews a system before it reaches a customer. Who runs it afterwards. If the answer to any of those is a team name rather than a person, the work will drift until someone senior gets nervous and stops it.

Choice comes first, and it is mostly a filter. A candidate process needs volume, a measurable outcome, and a tolerable failure mode. Volume, because a system used twice a week never accumulates enough signal to improve. A measurable outcome, because a metric you have to survey for cannot gate a release. A tolerable failure mode, because the first version will be wrong sometimes and you need to know what that costs.

Review comes second. It should be boring and written down: what evidence a launch needs, who signs, and what evidence would stop it. In practice this is a short checklist attached to the register entry, not a governance ceremony. The point is that the answer exists before someone needs it at eleven at night.

Ownership comes third and is the one that gets skipped. A pilot that reaches production without a named internal owner becomes shadow infrastructure: nobody updates it, nobody watches its cost, and its failure surprises everyone. Handover is a deliverable, not a formality, and it only counts once someone is actually watching the dashboard.

This is also why fractional works for companies of this size. You need the decisions made properly once, written down, and handed to someone inside the company. You do not need a permanent executive to maintain four documents and a review checklist. An engagement that does not end has usually replaced an operating model rather than built one.
Evals in CI for LLM agents, without a golden answer — meshin.co

An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one. A model provider’s silent update slips through every time. Putting an eval suite in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching.

Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent’s eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is.

Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. On only.help, my own product, the support-triage rollout built its first eval set from tickets already answered. It then found that the first week looked better than the system really was, purely from seasonal timing. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects. That mix is a sturdier base than one convenient week.

Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code that it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request. Change it through the same review a code change gets.

Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how the agent is actually used.

Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first.

Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs.

OWASP’s list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed. It should also check that the tool fires correctly when needed.

For the answer’s content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is simply not supported by anything the system looked at. That is the failure mode a plain accuracy score misses entirely.

Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor.

NIST’s AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute.

A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge’s own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage.

Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of surfacing it.

Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet.

When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build.

Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails.

Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it.

Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression. That holds even if every other score stays green. A 90-Day Production Sprint puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice.

A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log.

Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget can page an owner instead. So can a drop in judge-human agreement, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone’s memory of which checks are actually load-bearing.

Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.

Why your AI pilot never reached production — meshin.co

A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs: a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. They also lack a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does.

Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator.

Ownership is not a shared inbox or a Slack channel. It is one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it.

Most pilots reach a vendor’s API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes.

The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet.

A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move, such as tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task.

Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly.

Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider’s own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships, so a regression surfaces first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build.
That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. It is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off.
Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic; most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own.

For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses: a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover.

I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it.

Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An AI readiness and risk assessment is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo that names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move.

A 90-Day Production Sprint turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one, and the rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident.

The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge.
This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it.

Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence’s. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor is allowed to see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you.

It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask; it does not answer whether a specific vendor’s terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms.

The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test, not every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down, which is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do.

It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days; it does not shortcut them.

What is a conformity assessment? — meshin.co

A conformity assessment is the process a provider completes before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, either checking it internally or having an accredited outside body check it. It shows the system actually meets the EU AI Act's requirements, rather than merely claiming to.

For almost every high-risk system, the outcome is simple: the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off instead.

Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standards, the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance, are not fully applied or do not yet exist.

The assessment is not a one-time formality. Any substantial change to a system after launch triggers a new one, under whichever route applied the first time. The one exception is a system that keeps learning after deployment. A provider can plan for that drift in advance and record it in the technical documentation before the first assessment. Later changes that stay within that plan do not reopen the process.

An investor or a board asks how a company knows its AI system is compliant, and a vague assurance is not the same as pointing to a completed assessment and a signed declaration. A procurement team increasingly asks to see evidence the assessment happened at all, rather than taking a compliance claim on trust. It also surfaces at the worst time, during a late-stage system change, when nobody planned for a second assessment.

Work out early, before the system is built, which assessment route applies, since a notified-body review takes far longer to arrange than an internal one and cannot be rushed at launch. Keep the assessment evidence alongside the technical documentation it depends on, not in a file only one person can find. Mapping each system to its likely route is part of the AI readiness and risk assessment done before a deadline forces the decision.
What is data classification? — meshin.co

NIST's own method for federal systems ties each category to a real question, not a subjective label: what actually happens to confidentiality, integrity or availability if this breaks, meaning who could see this data, alter it, or take it offline? A scheme built the same way works for AI. That is what makes classification useful for a real decision, not a compliance exercise nobody consults.

Every additional tool a company adopts multiplies the places a given tier could leak from. That is why the scheme has to live inside the AI register, not beside it. Without one, two employees facing the same document reach different answers. The wrong answer usually only surfaces after the data has already left the building through a chat prompt.

It is the first practical question underneath any AI acceptable-use policy. Can this go into that tool? Nobody can answer that until someone has labelled what this actually is. A security reviewer asks for the classification scheme by name, not as an abstract principle. The scheme is what turns a policy from a statement of intent into something an employee can actually follow on a Tuesday afternoon.

Keep the scheme small. Three or four tiers is enough for most companies, and a scheme nobody can remember gets ignored the same as none. Map every AI tool in the register to which tiers may reach it. Make the most important rule explicit: customer data and secrets never go into an unclassified tool. The AI Governance Starter Kit already includes this table, mapped to what may reach a vendor.
