What is a DPIA? — meshin.co
DPIA

GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default.

It has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, that officer must be consulted while the assessment is carried out. Signing off afterward does not count.

Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 points the other way too. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

Almost any AI system worth building processes personal data, which makes a DPIA the default question rather than an edge case, and legal or procurement asks for it specifically once a system moves from a prototype to something touching real customer records. It gets confused with the newer AI Act impact assessment often enough that clarifying the difference is usually the more useful answer than either document alone.

Write the DPIA before the system is built, not after, since a risk found during design is cheap to change and the same risk found after launch usually is not. Start from what is actually being collected and why, not from a template’s headings, and consult the data protection officer while there is time to act. The AI Governance Starter Kit lays out the same data classification a DPIA starts from.
What is the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. Everything else is left largely unregulated.

Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there, which is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem.

In practice, it changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight, with evidence of both ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

It comes up the moment a company has, or wants, a customer in the EU, regardless of where it is based. A customer’s legal team asks which risk tier your product falls into before they sign, because their own exposure depends on your answer. A board asks about it once a competitor gets fined, or a customer raises it at renewal. The Act follows the AI system’s users, not the provider’s registered address.

Work out which risk tier each AI system falls into. Most products used inside a normal business are not high-risk, but a few categories, hiring and credit among them, almost always are and deserve a real legal read. For anything near the high-risk category, start the paperwork now: a risk assessment, a named oversight point, and technical documentation. For everything else, keep the register entry current, so the answer is a lookup, not a scramble.
What are evals? — meshin.co
Evals
Evals are repeatable tests that score an AI system's outputs against a fixed set of examples and criteria, run before release and again whenever the prompt, data or model changes.

The comparison that matters is to an ordinary test suite. There is one difference: the system under test can give a different answer each run. A typical eval is a set of inputs with known good answers or a scoring rule. It runs automatically whenever the prompt, the model or the surrounding code changes, with a pass rate tracked over time rather than a single pass or fail.

Engineering teams build them because "it worked when I tried it a few times" does not survive a prompt change six months later, once nobody remembers which cases mattered. Security reviewers and boards ask about them because an eval suite is the concrete answer to "how do you know it still works," which otherwise has no answer better than trust.
In practice, evals change how a team ships. A prompt or model change runs through the same suite every time, and a drop in the pass rate blocks a release the same way a failing test would.

A security reviewer or a technical board member asks the same question they would of any release process: what stops a bad change from reaching customers. For a normal codebase, the answer is a test suite. For an AI feature, the honest answer is either an eval suite or “we check by hand.” That second answer does not hold up once a product has more than a couple of prompts.

Write down twenty to fifty real cases the system must handle correctly. Draw them from actual support tickets or usage, not invented examples, and include a few you know are hard. Score each case automatically where you can, and by a human reviewer where you cannot. Track the pass rate over time rather than treating one run as final. Run the suite before every prompt or model change ships.
What are guardrails in an AI system? — meshin.co
Guardrails

Guardrails are the checks placed around what an AI model can be asked, what it can say, and what it can do. They are enforced in the surrounding code, not left to the model's training. That way an unusual input cannot simply talk the system out of a rule.

In practice a guardrail is one of three things: a topic restriction on what the model will engage with, or an output filter on what a user sees. The third, an action gate, controls what the system may do without a check first.

OWASP, an independent security-standards group, publishes its own mitigation list for prompt injection, which reads like a checklist for these three. Privilege control and human approval for high-risk actions are guardrails, not model behaviour.

This is closer to what NIST's AI Risk Management Framework calls its Manage function: turning a risk decision into something the system enforces, not something merely written down. Guardrails are how that function shows up in code, not in a policy document nobody checks against production.

Asking what guardrails a system has is one of the shortest, most common questions in a security review. It is a hard one to answer honestly if the only guardrail is the model’s own training and good manners. A board hears it as a proxy for a bigger question: what is the actual worst thing this system could be tricked into doing? And what stands between that action and a real customer?

Write guardrails as rules the code enforces, not text pasted into a prompt. Test each one against an input designed to defeat it, not a well-behaved example. Put a real check in front of any action that spends money, changes a record, or sends something external. That way a failure blocks the action instead of completing it. The 90-Day Production Sprint builds these checks into the workflow itself, not as a retrofit after an incident.
What is a hallucination rate? — meshin.co
A hallucination rate is the share of a model's answers that state something false or invented in the same confident tone as a correct one, measured against questions with known correct answers.

NIST's generative-AI risk guidance calls this failure confabulation, distinct from an ordinary software bug because confidence is never a reliable guide to accuracy here. That makes it different from a crash or an error message, which at least announces itself. A model rarely answers "I don't know": left to guess, it produces a fluent answer instead, which is why the rate has to be measured rather than assumed.

Measuring it means running the model against questions with known correct answers. The score is how often the answer is invented rather than true, the same discipline an eval suite already applies to other kinds of failure. That turns a vague worry into a tracked number.

A board asks this before it asks about model architecture or vendor choice. It turns “is the AI any good” into a number anyone can track quarter to quarter. A company that cannot answer with one, measured on its own real use cases, is really saying “we do not know.” That reads differently in a board pack than an honest figure with the method stated plainly.

Measure the rate on the eval suite’s real cases, not a generic public benchmark. Behaviour on general trivia says little about a specific product’s actual questions. Track the number after every prompt or model change, the way an eval pass rate is tracked. Do not measure it once and assume it holds. The 90-Day Production Sprint puts this measurement inside continuous integration, so a regression blocks a release.
What makes an AI system high-risk? — meshin.co

A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of, or itself, a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, such as medical devices or machinery. That underlying law already requires third-party conformity assessment.

Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk for landing in one of those areas alone, with no product-safety law involved at all.

A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task: reformatting an application into a standard template, say. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing its recommendation.

A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at them. None of the four survives contact with profiling: a system that profiles individual people is high-risk regardless.

It is the first question every other AI Act obligation depends on. A customer’s legal team or an investor’s due diligence checklist asks it before anything else about the system. A board hears it phrased more simply, as “are we in the category that gets the heavy paperwork, and who decided.” Getting the classification wrong either way has a real cost, either missed obligations or needless process on a system that never required it.

Run the classification test on each system separately, not on the company as a whole. One product can be high-risk while another, built the same month, is not. Write the decision down, including the reasoning for a not-high-risk conclusion, since an authority can ask to see it later. This classification is exactly what the AI readiness and risk assessment produces for every system in the inventory, not just the ones already suspected.
What is human-in-the-loop? — meshin.co
Human-in-the-loop
Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or can stop an AI system's output before it takes effect, rather than the system acting on its own once it starts.

The concept sits on a spectrum, from full autonomy at one end to human-on-the-loop at the other, where a person can intervene but does not have to act. Human-in-the-loop sits in between: a person must actively approve each step before it happens.

Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. It is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about, for anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing.

Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and where it still needs one.

It comes up whenever an AI system’s decision touches something real: a loan, a job application, a support case, a medical or safety-adjacent judgement. A customer’s legal team wants to know whether a person can catch and correct a bad output before it reaches someone affected. That is not the same as a person being “involved” in some vague sense. A board asks after seeing an automated system make a costly call nobody had reviewed.

Decide, system by system, where full automation is fine, a wrong answer that costs little and is easy to reverse. Decide, too, where a person must review before anything takes effect. Where a person is in the loop, give them enough time and context to catch a bad output. A rubber-stamp screen that exists only to tick a box does not count. Record which category each system falls into in the AI register.
What does human oversight require under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

Article 14 splits the mechanism into two kinds of measure. Some are built into the system itself by the provider before it ships. An example is an interface that flags a low-confidence output. Others are measures the provider identifies for the deployer to carry out instead, such as a rule about when a person must review a case before it proceeds.

Article 14 spells out five specific capacities the overseeing person needs. They must understand the system's real limits well enough to spot a malfunction, and stay alert to automation bias rather than trusting the output by default. They also need to correctly read what the output actually means, disregard or reverse a specific output when needed, and have a way to halt the system outright.

It differs from asking whether a human is in the loop. That is a design question about where a person sits in a workflow. Human oversight is a legal test of whether that person is equipped to catch a bad output, with the time, context and authority to stop it. An auditor tests this by asking what the overseer would do in a specific bad case, not whether a review step exists on a diagram.

Name the specific person or role authorised to halt each high-risk system, not a team, and check they have time per case to evaluate output rather than approve on reflex. Train that person specifically on automation bias. A rushed or over-trusting reviewer defeats the requirement even when the process looks correct. The Fractional CAIO Retainer includes reviewing who watches each system, and whether they could catch a failure this week.
What is ISO/IEC 42001? — meshin.co
ISO/IEC 42001

ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence published it in December 2023. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security.

Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard a company can be audited and certified against by an accredited third party. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask where you sit against it, because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim.

In practice, working towards it means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. None of that requires certification itself.

A procurement team building a vendor shortlist asks for it by name. A board that already understands ISO 27001 reaches for the same mental model, and asks whether an AI equivalent exists. Because it is a certifiable standard, not a public framework, it carries more weight in a formal audit than a self-written policy. That is why a customer’s legal team may put it on a checklist before reading what is in it.

Full certification is a real project with an external auditor, and most companies at seed to growth stage do not need it yet. What is worth doing now is running the standard’s own structure without the audit: a documented risk-assessment method, an AI system inventory, and a review of that inventory on a fixed schedule. That gives you “built to the same structure, without the certificate,” a stronger position than silence or an unsupported claim.
What is an LLM gateway? — meshin.co

Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. Through that point, a company can control who is allowed to call a model. It can log every prompt and response for an audit trail, and redact sensitive data before it leaves the building. It can also apply rate and cost limits, and fail over to a different provider if one goes down.

Without a gateway, API keys end up scattered across a codebase, and nobody holds a full log of what was sent to a vendor. A data leak through a prompt stays invisible until a customer or regulator finds it first.

Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. It also gives a direct, specific answer to a vendor questionnaire's question about how model access is controlled. That beats a description of several applications each doing it inconsistently.

A security questionnaire almost always asks how access to the model provider is controlled and logged. “Each team manages its own API key” is a poor answer. A board or customer asks a version of the same question after a well-publicised leak elsewhere, where a prompt carrying sensitive data reached a third-party model unlogged. Without a gateway, nobody can produce every prompt sent to a vendor last month.

Put one gateway in front of every model call before adding a second application that talks to a model, not after. Route all API keys through it rather than into individual codebases, and log every request and response. Redact anything that looks like a customer identifier or a secret before it leaves. Solid open-source and hosted options already exist, so this is rarely worth building in house.
What is a model card? — meshin.co

A model card is a short, standard-shaped document a model's maker publishes. It describes what the model was built for, and how it performs across groups and conditions. It also names where the model should not be used, closer to a spec sheet than a sales page.

The format comes from a 2018 paper. It proposed model cards as a response to models shipping with no consistent account of how they had actually been tested. A rigorous card reports evaluation broken out by group: race, geographic location, sex, skin type. It also breaks out intersections, such as age combined with race, instead of one blended figure that hides where performance drops.

NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a card has most likely skipped the evaluation itself, not just the paperwork describing it.

Procurement asks a model vendor for it directly once evaluating more than one option. A card makes two vendors comparable on the same axes, rather than on whatever each chose to advertise. A technical due-diligence review reads the limitations section specifically. That is where a vendor is most likely to have been honest about where the model actually struggles.

Ask every model vendor for their card before signing. Read the limitations section before the headline numbers: the numbers are chosen by the vendor, and the limitations rarely are. If a company fine-tunes or wraps a base model itself, write a short card of its own. Describe what changed and what was tested. The vendor questionnaire this request belongs in is one of the four documents in the AI Governance Starter Kit.
What is model provenance? — meshin.co

Article 53 of the EU AI Act turned this from a private claim into a published one for general-purpose models. Providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, following a template the AI Office issued. That summary covers the scale of the data, and whether it includes licensed material, scraped web content, user data or synthetic data.

For a smaller company building on someone else's model, provenance is a due-diligence question, not a publishing duty. Work through it before signing, not after. That distinction decides who actually reads the summary, and when: before a contract is signed, not after a customer's legal team goes looking for where the data came from.

A customer’s legal team asks it once a product’s output could plausibly end up in something they publish, resell or use to make a decision. They inherit whatever rights problem the underlying model carries. It also comes up quietly in procurement: which model is actually behind a feature can have a different answer than the vendor’s marketing page implies. That gap widens once a vendor swaps providers without telling anyone.

Ask every model vendor what the model was trained on, or where its training-data summary sits if the vendor owes one. Ask what licence covers the weights and output. Record the answer in the AI register next to that system, not in an email thread nobody can find during a review. Reading the actual vendor list, not asking a company to describe it from memory, is what the AI readiness and risk assessment does.
What is the NIST AI RMF? — meshin.co
NIST AI RMF

The framework sets out four functions an organisation applies to an AI system. GOVERN covers policy and accountability, while MAP covers understanding context and risk. Testing and metrics fall under MEASURE. Acting on what it found is MANAGE's job.

It is not a law, and it is not sector specific. A bank, a hospital and a ten-person startup can all use the same structure. US procurement teams, and increasingly non-US ones, ask about it because it gives a common vocabulary for a question that used to have no fixed answer: how you know an AI system's risks are actually managed, not just discussed once.
In practice, adopting it means someone can point to a specific function, and to a specific piece of evidence behind it. That beats a general assurance that everything is under control.

It comes up in almost every vendor security questionnaire, and in board packs once a company runs more than one AI system. A customer’s risk team wants a framework they recognise, not a bespoke description of your process, because it lets them compare you against every other vendor they review. A board wants the same thing for a different reason: a structure to ask questions against, rather than trusting that engineering thought of everything.

Read the four functions once, properly, rather than skimming a summary. Map what you already do against GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, and write down the gaps honestly. You do not need to implement all of it before you can talk about it. A short document listing what you have, your review step, and what you still owe against each function beats a claim of full compliance with nothing behind it.
What is observability for an AI system? — meshin.co
Observability

Observability is the ability to see, after the fact, exactly what a live AI system was asked. For any one case someone points to, it also shows what the system retrieved or called, and what it answered. An aggregate chart alone cannot explain one specific customer's bad experience.

For an agentic workflow, a system that also calls tools to look things up or take actions on its own, the record has to extend further. It needs every tool call made along the way, and what each one returned, not just the final input and output. A wrong outcome usually traces back to one step in a longer chain. Skipping tool-call logging leaves exactly that step unrecorded.

This differs from a simple uptime dashboard. It can show a system is running while saying nothing about whether one specific answer, given to one specific person, was actually right. NIST's risk management framework calls this its Measure function: a system only counts as measured if it keeps being tested and tracked after release, not just before.

A customer or an internal investigation asks: show me exactly what happened in this one case. A system with only aggregate metrics cannot answer. That is precisely the gap a security review is testing for when it asks about monitoring. It also comes up after a customer complaint that a specific answer was wrong. The honest response depends entirely on whether that exact exchange was ever recorded.

Log the full input, every step the system took including tool calls, and the output for every real request, not a sample. Keep those logs long enough to support an investigation. Make sure any one case can be pulled up by its own reference, rather than only appearing inside an average. This logging, plus a cost-per-outcome view, ships from the first release in the 90-Day Production Sprint.
What is post-market monitoring under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

Article 72 requires a documented monitoring system, sized to the technology and the risk of the specific system. It has to actively and systematically collect and analyse data on how the system performs once it is actually in use. Deployers feed into it directly, since Article 26 requires them to monitor the system on their end and report back to the provider. That way, the provider is not relying on its own visibility alone.

The monitoring plan is not a separate document. Article 72 makes it part of the system's technical documentation, built and updated alongside it, not bolted on after a complaint. A pattern the monitoring turns up is also the raw material for the next duty in the chain: deciding whether what happened counts as a serious incident that has to be reported.

Does anyone keep watching this system, or was it tested once and left alone? That is the specific question a customer’s security team or a regulator asks after any AI failure story in the press. A board hears it as reassurance that a problem would surface through a defined process rather than a customer complaint reaching the news first. Providers who can only describe pre-launch testing, and nothing after, usually have no answer.

Write the monitoring plan before launch - what gets measured, who reviews it, how often - since a plan invented after a problem appears is not the same thing. Build a route for deployer-reported issues to reach the provider.

A monitoring system that never hears from the people using it day to day is monitoring very little. The Fractional CAIO Retainer I run keeps this review on a fixed schedule, not only when a customer complains.
What is prompt injection? — meshin.co

Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text.

It has kept that position through every edition of the list, most recently the 2026 revision. The reason is structural: the model reads instructions and untrusted data through the same channel. A filter tuned on known patterns still misses a novel phrasing. Every mitigation available today reduces the odds of a successful attack; none removes them.

It is the first thing a security reviewer probes on any AI feature that reads outside content. That means a webpage, an uploaded file, an email, or a customer’s own message history. The concern is not academic. A model that can also send an email, issue a refund or query a database turns a successful injection into something already done. It is no longer just an embarrassing reply.

Never let a model’s output directly trigger a sensitive action without a check enforced in code. Keep the model’s own permissions to the smallest set it needs. Treat anything the model reads from outside the conversation as untrusted input, the way a web application treats a user-supplied string. Evals for exactly this kind of attack belong in the same pipeline that gates every other change. That is how I structure the 90-Day Production Sprint.
What is the difference between a provider and a deployer? — meshin.co
Provider vs deployer is the EU AI Act split between the company that builds an AI system and the company that runs it. Most of the Act's paperwork depends on which of the two roles a company holds.

Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. Giving the system away under your own brand still makes you the provider.

A deployer is defined by use, not branding: using the system under the deployer's own authority. The only carve-out is personal, non-professional activity. A company using a tool internally is a deployer even if it never touches a customer.

That test has a sharp edge. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the company actually wrote.

It surfaces in a contract negotiation once both sides realise the label matters more than expected, because a provider owes technical documentation and a conformity assessment while a deployer mainly owes human oversight and monitoring. A board hears about it when a vendor’s contract quietly assigns the company duties it assumed the vendor carried. Getting the role wrong can leave a company holding an obligation nobody budgeted for.

Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company, since rebranding one vendor’s model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. Write the answer into the AI register alongside the risk tier, since a security questionnaire will eventually ask for both. The Fractional CAIO Retainer is where I answer this kind of question inside a live negotiation.
What is red teaming for an AI system? — meshin.co

A red team engagement produces a different kind of output than a test run. It is a list of the specific techniques that worked, detailed enough for someone else to reproduce the failure. It also carries a judgement on what an attacker could actually do with it. That reproducibility is what separates a report from an anecdote about something that broke once.

NIST's generative AI profile recommends red teaming as a check against specific categories of harm, including information leakage and harmful content generation. Those failures depend on someone actively trying to cause them; they rarely show up in ordinary use. The finding that matters is the one nobody predicted going in.

Boards and security reviewers increasingly ask for it by name, rather than accepting “we ran evals” as a full answer. An eval suite built by the same team that built the system tends to test what that team already expected to go wrong. It matters more, not less, once a system can take actions or read outside content. A missed failure then moves from a bad reply to a completed action.

Budget real time, not an afternoon, for someone to actively try prompt injection, data extraction and off-limits requests. Do it against the actual live system, not a sanitised demo. Write down exactly what broke, and fix the underlying guardrail, not just the one example that happened to get tried. I treat this as part of shipping in the 90-Day Production Sprint, folding findings back into the eval suite before launch.
What is retrieval augmented generation? — meshin.co

The document store is usually a vector index. Passages are converted into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and a query is matched against them by similarity, not exact keyword. That is what lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document.

OWASP, the group that publishes widely used security-risk lists, tracks this as its own risk category. In a shared vector database, one customer's data can leak into another customer's results. Embeddings themselves can sometimes be inverted, too, to recover the source text they were built from. Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

Procurement asks “is this RAG, or did you train on our data,” because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer’s content into the model’s own weights. It also comes up once accuracy is questioned. A wrong answer usually traces to a retrieval problem, not a flaw in the model itself.

Control access at the document-store level, not only at the chat interface. RAG will surface anything in the index to anyone who can ask the right question, regardless of who is meant to see it. Treat the document store itself as a data-classification boundary. Check what happens when a document containing hidden instructions ends up inside it. That exact scenario is one of the checks in the 90-Day Production Sprint.
What counts as a serious incident under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

The duty falls on the provider, the company that built the system, and sometimes on the deployer, the company running it. It applies once a malfunction leads to death, serious harm, or a serious breach of someone's fundamental rights.

Article 73 fixes the clock in days, not in vague urgency. The default is fifteen days from when the provider becomes aware of the incident. A widespread infringement or a serious disruption to critical infrastructure tightens that to two days. A death tightens it further, to ten days. Every deadline runs from awareness, not from the incident itself.

Once the report is filed, the provider has to investigate: assess the risk, take corrective action, and cooperate with the authority. It cannot alter the system in a way that would affect the investigation's findings without telling the authority first. The duty also covers serious harm to property or the environment, not only harm to people, though that case still runs on the fifteen-day default.

It surprises companies who assume that deploying a high-risk system is a one-time compliance exercise, the same way a data-breach notification law surprises a company that has never had to report one before. A board’s real question is usually simpler - if something goes badly wrong, does the company already know who calls the regulator, or would that decision be made live, under pressure, by whoever happens to be in the room.

Decide in advance, in writing, who has the authority to judge that an incident is serious enough to report, rather than leaving that call to whoever notices the problem first. Preserve the system’s state at the time of the incident for investigation, instead of immediately patching it away. What is shadow AI? — meshin.co
Shadow AI is any AI tool an employee uses for company work without IT or security's knowledge. Examples range from a personal chatbot account to a browser extension or a locally run model.

The hardest form to spot is a model downloaded and run locally on a laptop. It never crosses the network as a request to a known AI vendor. The same problem shows up wherever an employee reaches for a tool without asking. A developer might call a model's API directly from a side project. A browser extension might quietly send page content to a third party to generate its summary.

None of it sits inside a contract governing how that vendor handles company or customer data, because no one negotiated one. None of it appears in the AI register either. A security review or an incident response then starts from a blind spot, not a known list. The tool itself is rarely the real risk. The missing record of its use is.

It is usually the first uncomfortable finding of a readiness assessment, and nobody did anything malicious. The register a company thought was complete turns out to have gaps. That happens the moment someone checks browser extensions and expense reports, instead of asking teams to self-report. A customer’s security team asks about it, having been burned before. A board hears one checkable question: could an employee be pasting customer data into a public tool right now?

Look rather than ask: check browser extension inventories, expense reports for AI subscriptions, and API billing for model providers nobody remembers approving. Publish a short list of approved tools, and a fast route to request a new one. The main driver of shadow AI is an approval process slower than the problem it solves. Fold anything found straight into the AI register, rather than treating discovery and governance as separate steps.
What is a sub-processor? — meshin.co
Sub-processor

A sub-processor is a vendor an AI provider hands a company's data to behind the scenes. The model provider behind a SaaS tool is a common example. GDPR Article 28 requires the provider to get the customer's permission, and to bind the sub-processor to the same data protections by contract.

GDPR Article 28 calls the AI vendor the processor and your company the controller. It gives the processor two ways to bring a sub-processor in. Specific authorisation names the sub-processor up front, so the controller signs off by name.

General authorisation lets the processor add sub-processors as needed, but it has to tell the controller first and give a real chance to object. Either way, the processor must pass down the same data-protection obligations it owes directly, in the contract itself, not just a notice.

The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops sit between a company's data and the last party that can actually see it.

It is a routine line on a security questionnaire: “list your sub-processors.” It is also a revealing one. Most AI features are built on someone else’s model, which makes a sub-processor almost guaranteed rather than an edge case. A buyer who skips the question is signing a contract blind. They will not know where their data actually goes once it leaves the vendor’s own systems.

Ask every AI vendor for its sub-processor list, and how it notifies customers of a change. Then check honestly: does the notice give a real chance to object, or just a record that it happened? Fold the answer into the AI register entry for that vendor, next to the data classification of what reaches them. What is technical documentation under the EU AI Act? — meshin.co

The EU AI Act sets the content directly in Annex IV, rather than leaving it to the provider's judgement. A national authority or notified body has to be able to assess it without relying on the provider's own explanation. Article 11 lets a small or micro enterprise use a simplified version of the same form, one the Commission publishes for that purpose.

Article 18 sets how long it has to survive: ten years from when the system was placed on the market or put into service. A national competent authority can request it at any point in that window. The same retention duty covers the quality management system records and the EU declaration of conformity too, not the technical documentation alone.

It is different from a marketing spec sheet or an engineering wiki page, and a regulator or notified body wants the specific content the Act lists, not a general description of the product. It also comes up in procurement due diligence, where a buyer of a high-risk system sometimes asks to see excerpts before signing. A vendor who can produce none of it has told you something.

Start the document on the first day of build, recording design decisions as they are made, since reconstructing the reasoning behind a choice months later is far harder than writing it down at the time. Version it alongside the system itself, so the documentation for a given release actually matches what shipped.
